abstract: The relating of product specifications to measurement standards must be undertaken with great care. It is very easy to overlook important sections of the product performance particularly in the so called 'Grey' areas and at the borders and limits of the specification. Many users however seem to use the products in these 'Grey' areas to make measurements sometimes oblivious of the risks they are taking. Unfortunately, there is no easy solution to the of problem of relating product specifications to measurement standards. It is necessary to pay careful attention how the individual parts of the specification are used and combined to demonstrate the product performance.

abstract: All measurements are tainted by imperfectly known errors, so the significance associated with the result of a measurement must account for this uncertainty. This paper explores the reasoning behind, and the requirements for, the expression of a value of uncertainty associated with a measurement result.

articleTitle: Pro-forma worked examples on uncertainty in electrical measurement
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium Uncertainties Workshop - Electrical Measurements (Ref. No. 1998/458)
abstract: Most measurements made in the electrical field will be subject to errors of some kind, however small. A measured value should therefore be stated with a corresponding measurement uncertainty to define the probable limits of variation in the result. This paper is aimed at describing the logic and use of pro-forma methods for the calculation of formal uncertainty budgets for the more common instrument based measurement facilities, such as calibrators and DMMs, albeit the technique may be applied to most measurement situations.

articleTitle: European and international standards for derivation and statements of uncertainties
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium Uncertainties Workshop - Electrical Measurements (Ref. No. 1998/458)
abstract: Modern well-developed high technologies need "precise measurements" standing for high reproducibility in performance or operation of products and parts. Today's strong national and international interconnections in trade and industry require traceability of measures. Traceability is the property of the result of a measurement whereby it can be related in a clear and well-defined way to appropriate standards, generally national or international ones, and by these to the conventional units through an unbroken chain of comparisons. This means that comparison of values is needed on nearly each level. In order to compare values, one needs a judgement on the reliability of those values, in short terms, a statement of quality. Such a statement will be based on scientific knowledge, i.e. based on objective facts which can be inspected, but as a judgement it is always subjective in nature. General acceptance of a judgement may be achieved, however, if the way how the statement has been generated becomes transparent, so that every one can redo and understand its details. It is the objective of this talk to compile some fundamental concepts and terms involved in setting up a quality statement in metrology.
